extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys, agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement and best mode) and related utility (35 U.S.C. 101) issues during patent examination, including use of affidavits, prior art, claim scope, and procedures for making rejections. Intended to direct examiner analyses and applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit evidence for enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual evidence directed to the amount of time and effort and level of knowledge required for the practice of the invention from the disclosure, and knowledge in the art can be expected to rebut a prima facie case of nonenablement, but not opinion evidence directed to the ultimate legal question of enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits that merely state conclusions (e.g., 'could be constructed', 'capable of being programmed', or that a skilled person 'could design or construct') fail unless buttressed by facts. Relevant factual detail includes e.g., number of programmers needed, number of man-hours, and level of skill required. An affidavit that describes learning the invention from the inventor (rather than from the application as filed) is not probative of enablement. Affiant testimony must be probative of the level of skill in the art as of the time the applicant filed the application (see Hirschfield; In re Brown; In re Gunn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercially-available prior art systems and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial availability of an identified prior art computer system is very pertinent to the issue of enablement, but in some cases this approach may not be sufficient to meet the applicant’s burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely citing excerpts from technical publications or a commercially-available system is insufficient unless it is made clear which parts/which circuits could be used and how they would be interconnected to construct the claimed device. Analysis is less critical where the circuits are essentially standard components of an identified prior art computer system and a standard device attached thereto (see In re Forman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior patents/publications as evidence of state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art patents and patent application publications are often relied upon to show the state of the art for purposes of enablement, but such documents must have a publication date earlier than the effective filing date of the application under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents issued after the filing date are not evidence of what was known to persons skilled in the art at the filing date. When relying on cited patents to show particular components are 'old', the examiner must analyze whether such patents are germane and whether they provide better disclosure detail than the applicant’s own disclosure. Cited patents/publications showing a programming technique is 'well-known' do not establish that one of ordinary skill could make the disclosed programming techniques unless both are of approximately the same degree of complexity (see In re Budnick; In re Gunn; In re Knowlton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments of counsel are not substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments of counsel alone cannot take the place of evidence in the record once an examiner has advanced a reasonable basis for questioning the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel's arguments or opinions are insufficient where factual support could be provided; factual affidavits would be appropriate. Where the record consists substantially of arguments and opinions of applicant’s attorney, the court has indicated that factual affidavits could have provided important evidence on enablement (see In re Budnick; In re Schulze; In re Cole; In re Knowlton; In re Wiseman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between utility (35 U.S.C. 101) and enablement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as to how to use the invention is different from the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101. 35 U.S.C. 101 requires that some specific, substantial, and credible use be set forth; 35 U.S.C. 112(a) requires an indication of how the invention can be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclosed specific and substantial utility alone does not guarantee compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) if undue experimentation would be required to practice the claimed invention. To avoid confusion, rejections under 112(a) based on grounds other than lack of utility should be imposed separately from any rejection under 101 (see MPEP § 2107 et seq.).

rubrics_metrics.name: When utility requirement is not satisfied (operative/useful)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim fails to meet the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101 because it is shown to be nonuseful or inoperative, then it necessarily fails to meet the how-to-use aspect of the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should make both rejections (under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a)) where subject matter is shown to be nonuseful/inoperative (see In re Fouche). The 112(a) rejection should indicate that because the invention lacks utility, a skilled person would not be able to use it as claimed. Office personnel should not impose a 112(a) rejection grounded on 'lack of utility' unless a proper 101 rejection is also made and factual showing for 101 is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden and applicant rebuttal on utility
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner concludes an application claims an invention that is nonuseful, inoperative, or contradicts known scientific principles, the burden is on the examiner to provide a reasonable basis to support this conclusion; if a proper 101 rejection is imposed, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No predetermined amount or character of evidence is required from the applicant; the character and amount vary depending on what is claimed and whether asserted utility appears to contravene established principles. Applicant's evidence must make the asserted utility more likely than not true; proof 'beyond a reasonable doubt' is not required (see In re Oetiker; Ex parte Ferguson; In re Irons; In re Fisher; In re Swartz; In re Brana).

rubrics_metrics.name: When utility is shown but invention is not enabled
rubrics_metrics.description: In some instances the utility of the claimed invention will be provided, but the skilled artisan will not know how to effect that use; in such a case no rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 will be made, but a rejection will be made under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention may have great utility yet the specification may fail to enable one skilled in the art to use it (Mowry v. Whitney). Examiners should evaluate enablement separately from utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: All questions of enablement are evaluated against the claimed subject matter — whether everything within the scope of the claim is enabled. The focus is whether the specification teaches how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without 'undue experimentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine exactly what is encompassed by the claims (consider each claim as a whole; dependent claims incorporate limitations per 35 U.S.C. 112(d)). The specification need not disclose well-known matter. The scope of enablement must bear a 'reasonable correlation' to the scope of the claims. If claims are broader than the enabling disclosure, the examiner should identify what subject matter is considered enabled (see AK Steel; In re Wright; In re Fisher; Plant Genetic Sys.; Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner identification of enabled subject matter when claiming broader than disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rejection is made based on the view that the enablement is not commensurate in scope with the claim, the examiner should identify the subject matter that is considered to be enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations and examples in the specification do not generally limit the claims; however the record must be clear so the public has notice of the patentee's scope of protection. The examiner should articulate the specific unenabled portions of the claimed scope to justify a 112(a) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single means claim enablement (single means recitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single means claim, i.e., where a means recitation does not appear in combination with another recited element of means, is subject to an enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) if the claim covers every conceivable means for achieving the stated purpose while the specification discloses at most only those means known to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims have been held nonenabling for scope of the claim (see In re Hyatt). When claims depend on a recited property, a comparable situation can arise (claim covers every conceivable structure for a stated property while spec discloses only those known to the inventor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperative subject matter within claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of inoperative embodiments within the scope of a claim does not necessarily render a claim nonenabled; the standard is whether a skilled person could determine which embodiments are operative with no more effort than is normally required in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prophetic examples do not make the disclosure nonenabling. Although inoperative embodiments are typically excluded by claim language, claims may still be nonenabled if undue experimentation is required to determine operable embodiments. A disclosure of many operable embodiments plus identification of a single inoperative one did not render claim nonenabled where undue experimentation was not involved. However, claims reading on significant numbers of inoperative embodiments may be nonenabled if the specification does not clearly identify operable embodiments (see Atlas Powder; In re Angstadt; In re Cook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical feature taught but not claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: A feature which is taught as critical in a specification and is not recited in the claims should result in a rejection of such claim under the enablement provision of 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine criticality by considering the entire disclosure; 'preferred' features are not necessarily 'critical.' An enablement rejection based on a missing critical limitation should be made only when the specification language makes clear the limitation is critical for the invention to function. Broad language in the disclosure, including the abstract, tends to rebut criticality (see In re Mayhew; In re Goffe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement — statutory statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor (pre-AIA language: 'The specification... shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best mode requirement prevents inventors from obtaining patent protection while withholding their preferred embodiment. Determining compliance requires (1) a subjective inquiry whether at filing the inventor possessed a best mode, and (2) an objective inquiry whether the written description disclosed the best mode such that a person skilled in the art could practice it (see Eli Lilly v. Barr). Failure to disclose the best mode need not rise to active concealment. Note: AIA amended enforcement (35 U.S.C. 282) so failure to disclose best mode is no longer a basis to cancel/invalid a claim in litigation, but the best mode requirement remains part of examination practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode specifics — what is/ is not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations relevant to best mode include: determine what the invention is (claims define invention); a specific example is not required; designation as 'best mode' is not required; updating the best mode is not required in certain priority contexts; a defect in best mode cannot be cured by adding new matter after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclaimed matter unrelated to operation of claimed invention does not trigger best mode. Absence of a working example is not determinative; best mode may be a preferred range or group. There is no statutory requirement that applicants point out which embodiment is best. Updating best mode is not required for foreign priority or certain benefit claims. Adding a specific mode after filing is treated as new matter and should be objected to (see In re Bosy; In re Gay; In re Honn; Ernsthausen; Standard Oil; In re Hay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode compared to enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The best mode requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement. Best mode requires enabling one of ordinary skill to practice the best mode, whereas enablement aims to place the claimed subject matter generally in the public's possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best mode is concerned with disclosure of applicant's recognized best way to practice the invention at time of filing; if applicant developed specific instrumentalities or techniques recognized as the best way, best mode requires disclosure of that information in addition to general enablement (see In re Newton; Spectra-Physics v. Coherent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for making a rejection for lack of best mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should assume that the best mode is disclosed unless evidence to the contrary is presented; a proper best mode analysis has two components: (A) subjective — did the inventor know at filing of a mode considered better than others; (B) objective — is the disclosure adequate to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first component is subjective and requires evidence that at the time of filing the inventor had information in possession indicating a mode was considered better. If the first component is not satisfied, there is no basis to address the second component or to make a best mode rejection. The second component is objective and depends on the level of skill in the art. Best mode rejections are extremely rare in ex parte prosecution because necessary evidence is rarely accessible to the examiner (see Chemcast; MPEP § 2165.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope analysis for enablement (claim-as-a-whole; dependent claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should determine what each claim recites and what the subject matter is when the claim is considered as a whole, not when its parts are analyzed individually. No claim should be overlooked; dependent claims incorporate limitations of the claims to which they refer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing enabled scope, keep claims' broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification in mind. Do not read everything in the specification into the claims; but ensure the full scope of the claim is enabled. Examples from case law (AK Steel, Amgen, In re Wright, etc.) illustrate when broad generic claims were found not commensurate with limited enabling disclosure.
